guide.title: Product packaging design in India: a practical guide for 2026
guide.metaDescription: How packaging works in 2026: the shelf, the thumbnail and the delivery box, India's mandatory label declarations, planning steps, mistakes and measures.
guide.lead: A pack has to protect the product, meet labeling law, stand out beside competitors and still read clearly as a small image on a phone. This guide explains how to plan for all of those jobs before a single design is drawn.

sections.heading: What packaging design covers
paragraphs: Packaging design is three disciplines working on one object. **Structure** is the physical format, whether a carton, pouch, jar, label or mailer, and how it opens, stacks and survives transport. **Graphics** are the brand, color, typography and imagery that make it recognizable. **Information** is everything the pack must say, from the product name and usage to the declarations the law requires.

Most problems come from handling these in sequence instead of together. A striking front panel that leaves no room for mandatory text, or a pouch size the printer cannot produce economically, sends the project back to the start.

sections.heading: Where packaging gets judged in 2026
paragraphs: Packs now meet customers in at least three settings, and each one tests the design differently.
Design for the hardest setting first. For many Indian D2C and FMCG brands that is now the thumbnail, so test every concept at the size a shopper sees in an app before judging it on a large monitor.
bullets: **The shelf:** seen from a couple of meters away among competitors, where color blocks and shape do most of the work.
**The thumbnail:** a small image in marketplace and quick-commerce search results, where fine print disappears and only the product name, variant and one strong visual survive.
**The doorstep:** the delivery box and what is inside it, which shapes first impressions for D2C brands and is often filmed for social media.

sections.heading: What the label must say in India
paragraphs: Labeling rules are not a finishing detail; they decide how much space you have to work with. Under the Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011, pre-packaged goods for retail sale must declare information such as the name and address of the manufacturer, packer or importer, country of origin, the common or generic name of the product, net quantity, month and year of manufacture, MRP, unit sale price, a best-before or use-by date where relevant, and consumer care details.

Packaged food must also follow FSSAI's labeling and display regulations of 2020. FSSAI's own FAQ states that the product name and the veg or non-veg logo belong on the front of the pack, that the FSSAI logo and license number must contrast with the background, and that allergens must be declared. Cosmetics, plastic packaging and exported goods each carry further rules.

Requirements depend on the product and change over time, so treat this as orientation rather than compliance advice. Have the final label text confirmed by your regulatory consultant or the relevant authority; the designer's job is to give that text a clear, legible place on the pack.

sections.heading: What has changed recently
paragraphs: None of these changes alter what good design is. They change how much information must fit, and where customers first see it.
bullets: **Unit sale price:** mandatory since January 1, 2024, so price panels need room for a per-unit figure, such as per kilogram or per gram, beside the MRP. A 2023 amendment exempted combination, group and multi-piece packages.

**A proposed wider scope:** in July 2024 the Department of Consumer Affairs proposed applying the rules to all packs sold at retail, including those above 25 kg. Check its current status if you sell large retail packs.

**Plastic packaging:** brand owners using plastic carry extended producer responsibility obligations, including registration details on the pack, and the rules on how that information appears have been revised more than once since 2024.
**Quick commerce:** fast-delivery apps have made the thumbnail as important as the shelf for snacks, personal care and household products.

sections.heading: How to plan a packaging project
paragraphs: Good packaging starts with a brief that settles practical questions before creative ones.
If the product or company is new, fix the brand basics first. Packaging designed before the brand's [identity is settled](/brand-development) often has to be redone within a year.
bullets: **Where will it sell?** Modern trade, kirana stores, marketplaces, your own website, export or gifting, ranked by importance.
**What sits beside it?** Photograph the shelf and screenshot the search results where your product will appear.
**What does production allow?** Get the printer's dieline, minimum order quantity, available materials and finishes before design begins.
**What must it say?** Collect the approved mandatory text, the claims you can substantiate and the barcodes.
**How many variants?** Plan a system for flavors, sizes or shades that grows without redesigning each one.

sections.heading: Common packaging mistakes
paragraphs: Each of these is far cheaper to catch in a 3D mockup or a printed sample than after a production run.
bullets: Designing on a flat screen and seeing the folded, filled pack only at the proof stage.
Adding mandatory text last, so it ends up in unreadable type or on a flap that folds out of sight.
Variant colors that look distinct on a monitor but nearly identical under store lighting.
Ignoring barcode size and clear space, which can cause scanning failures at the checkout.
Environmental claims the brand cannot substantiate, such as calling a pack recyclable when local systems cannot process it.
Approving color on screen rather than on a printed proof from the actual press and material.

sections.heading: How to measure whether packaging works
paragraphs: Packaging success shows up in sales and operations data, not just in compliments. Decide the measures before launch so you can compare old and new packs fairly.

Our [packaging process](/product-packaging-design/process) shows where each of these checks fits in a project, and a [product shoot](/shoot-services) turns the finished pack into listing and campaign images.
bullets: **Findability:** can people outside your team pick the product out of a shelf photo or a search results screenshot within a few seconds?
**Listing performance:** click-through and conversion on marketplace listings after the pack image changes.
**Retail acceptance:** feedback from distributors and store buyers, and whether new outlets agree to stock the range.
**Operational quality:** print errors, transit damage and returns linked to packaging.
**Unboxing response:** customer photos, videos and comments that mention the pack.

takeaways: Packaging is structure, graphics and information designed together, not one after another.
Test every concept at thumbnail size, because for many brands the phone screen is now the first shelf.
India's Legal Metrology rules and, for food, FSSAI's regulations decide how much space the mandatory text needs.
Get the printer's dieline, materials and minimum order quantity before design starts.
Approve color on a printed proof, never on a monitor.
Measure findability, listing performance, retail acceptance and damage, starting before launch.

faqs.q: Do I need a different pack design for marketplaces and quick commerce?
faqs.a: Usually not a different pack, but a design that holds up as a small image. Brands often add separate listing images that show the pack alongside key information, because marketplaces restrict what the main image may contain.

faqs.q: Who is responsible for getting the mandatory label text right?
faqs.a: The brand owner. A designer lays the text out clearly and checks it against the approved copy for legibility and completeness, but the content itself should come from your regulatory consultant or food technologist.

faqs.q: How many SKUs should share one design system?
faqs.a: Ideally all of them. A shared structure with a change of color, illustration or name per variant keeps the range recognizable, lowers design and print costs and makes adding a new variant quick.

faqs.q: Should we print a short run before the full order?
faqs.a: Where the printer allows it, yes, especially for a new material, finish or structure. A short run reveals color shifts, fit problems and transit damage that a digital mockup cannot show.

process.title: How we design product packaging, from brief to press-ready files
process.metaTitle: Our Packaging Design Process, Step by Step
process.metaDescription: How SmartWebCare designs packaging: channel brief, shelf and screen audit, structure and material, label hierarchy, concepts, SKU rollout and prepress.
process.lead: A packaging project involves your product team, your printer and your compliance advisor as well as us. The steps below show who does what, and what you receive before we move to the next stage.

steps.title: Product and channel brief
steps.summary: We learn the product, the price point and every place it will be sold, so the design is judged against the right settings.
activities: Run a workshop on the customer, competitors, price positioning and launch timeline
List the sales channels in priority order, from modern trade to marketplaces and gifting
Record production constraints such as cost per unit, minimum order quantities and packing equipment
steps.output: A signed-off packaging brief that every later decision is checked against.

steps.title: Shelf and screen audit
steps.summary: We study how your category looks in the places where customers actually choose.
activities: Photograph competitor shelves in relevant stores
Capture marketplace and quick-commerce search results for your category at phone size
Note the color codes, formats and claims the category already uses, and the gaps nobody occupies
steps.output: An audit board showing which category conventions to follow and which to break, with our recommendations.

steps.title: Structure and material
steps.summary: We choose the physical format with your printer or converter before any graphics are drawn.
activities: Compare formats such as cartons, pouches, labels, jars and mailers for protection, cost and shelf presence
Discuss materials and lower-impact options, with the trade-offs explained
Obtain the printer's dieline and physical samples
Plan the unboxing sequence for products shipped directly to customers
steps.output: An approved dieline and material specification, with samples where available.

steps.title: Label hierarchy and copy
steps.summary: We map every panel so the brand, the selling message and the mandatory information each get the space they need.
activities: Receive the approved declarations and claims from your compliance advisor
Decide what goes on the front, back and sides, in order of importance
Write front-of-pack naming and selling lines for your approval
steps.output: A copy deck and panel map, approved before visual design starts.

steps.title: Concepts and 3D mockups
steps.summary: We present a few distinct design directions as realistic mockups, viewed at shelf distance and at thumbnail size.
activities: Develop design routes from the audit and the brief
Render 3D mockups on the actual dieline
Show each route among competitor packs and inside a mocked-up search results screen
Gather structured feedback from your team and, where possible, a few customers
steps.output: A concept presentation and a chosen direction with agreed changes.

steps.title: Refinement and range rollout
steps.summary: We perfect the chosen design and extend it to every variant and pack size.
activities: Finalize typography, illustration and photography
Build the variant system for flavors, sizes or shades
Check mandatory text for legibility at actual print size
Prepare pack renders for your website and [marketplace listings](/marketplace-listings)
steps.output: Master artwork and approved files for the full range.

steps.title: Prepress and print support
steps.summary: We prepare files to the printer's specification and stay involved until the first production run is approved.
activities: Set colors as process or spot inks, with bleed, trapping and finish layers as the printer requires
Confirm barcode size and clear space with the printer
Review printed proofs against the approved artwork
Attend or review the press check where the printer allows it
steps.output: Print-ready files, signed-off proofs and a packaging spec sheet for future reprints.

deliverables: Master artwork and all variant files
Pack renders for your website and marketplaces
Packaging rules for future SKUs, ready to add to your [brand playbook](/brand-playbook)
youProvide: Product samples, dimensions and any existing packaging
Approved mandatory label text and claims from your regulatory or compliance advisor
An introduction to your printer or converter, or a request for us to suggest options
Brand assets: logo files, fonts, color references and guidelines
One decision-maker for concept and proof approvals

faqs.q: Can you work with our existing printer?
faqs.a: Yes, and we prefer to. Your printer's dieline, materials and press capabilities shape the design, so we involve them from the structure stage. If you need a printer, we can suggest options and compare quotes with you.

faqs.q: Do you write the mandatory label text?
faqs.a: No. We lay it out, check legibility and flag anything that looks missing, but the declarations themselves should come from your regulatory advisor. That keeps responsibility for compliance where it belongs.

faqs.q: What if the printed color doesn't match what we approved?
faqs.a: That is why we approve color on printed proofs from the actual material, not on screen. If a production run still drifts, we compare it with the signed proof and work with the printer on the correction. To plan your project, [book a consultation](/book-consultation).

useCases.title: Packaging design use cases: six product businesses and their packs
useCases.metaTitle: Packaging Design Use Cases for Brands
useCases.metaDescription: Illustrative packaging scenarios for snack, fragrance, spice, juice, hand-tool and festive sweets brands: the challenge, our approach and what to measure.
useCases.lead: Every packaging brief starts from a different problem: a crowded shelf, a fragile product, an export buyer or a festive deadline. These illustrative scenarios show how the approach changes and what each business should track.

cases.title: Standing out on the quick-commerce screen
cases.challenge: An Indore namkeen brand selling mainly through neighborhood stores is moving onto quick-commerce apps and into modern trade. Its pouches use a different look for each flavor, and in app search results the flavor names are unreadable.
approach: Create one pouch system with a fixed logo position and a bold color for each flavor
Enlarge the product and flavor names so they read at thumbnail size
Move mandatory declarations into a clear back-panel grid that fits every pouch size
Produce pack renders for each app listing, with support from our [marketplace listings](/marketplace-listings) team
measure: Listing conversion on quick-commerce apps before and after the change
Retail buyer feedback while onboarding new outlets

cases.title: Making the delivery box part of the product
cases.challenge: Perfume bottles arrive in plain shipping cartons with loose padding. Customers mention breakage in reviews, and almost nobody shares the unboxing.
approach: Design a branded mailer with a fitted insert that holds the bottle securely
Add a printed card explaining the scent notes and how to wear the fragrance
Send test packs through a real courier run before ordering in bulk
measure: Customer photos and videos of the unboxing

cases.title: Preparing a spice range for overseas shelves
cases.challenge: A spice company that sells in bulk wants retail packs for Indian grocery stores in the UK and the Gulf. Its current packs were designed only for Indian rules and Indian shoppers.
approach: Design a retail pouch and carton that tell the origin story clearly to shoppers abroad
Leave flexible label zones for importer details and destination-country requirements
Ask the exporter's compliance partner to confirm each market's rules before artwork is final
Choose barrier materials that protect aroma through long shipping times
measure: Acceptance by importers and store buyers
Shelf-life or quality complaints from overseas
Time needed to adapt the artwork for a new country

cases.title: Labeling a curved bottle that lives in a fridge
cases.challenge: Labels wrinkle on the round bottles and smudge from condensation in store fridges. With a short shelf life, dates are printed daily and must be easy to read.
approach: Work with the label printer on a moisture-resistant stock and adhesive
Lay out the front so the name and flavor read clearly on a curved surface
Design a clear area for date and batch coding on the production line
Check front-of-pack requirements with the brand's food technologist
measure: Labels lost or damaged in retail fridges
Sell-through by flavor in partner stores

cases.title: Helping dealers pick the right box
cases.challenge: A hand-tool maker sells through hardware dealers. Boxes for different sizes look almost identical, dealers pick the wrong one and customers return tools that do not fit their job.
approach: Introduce a size and type coding system using numbers, icons and color bands
Put a clear product photo and the key specifications on the front panel
Standardize carton labels so warehouse staff can identify stock quickly

cases.title: Creating a festive gift box on a deadline
cases.challenge: A sweets brand wants a Diwali gift box for retail and corporate orders, with only weeks before production. It must look premium, protect the sweets and stay within a sensible cost per unit.
approach: Choose a rigid or folding carton format the printer can deliver in the time available
Design an outer sleeve that changes each festival while the inner box stays the same
Add a separate card for corporate logos or personal messages
Confirm food-contact materials and labeling with the brand's food safety advisor
measure: Corporate gifting inquiries and repeat orders
Reuse of the inner box in the next festive season

faqs.q: Our product is still in development. Is it too early for packaging?
faqs.a: It is a good time to start structure and material discussions, because they affect product size, fill and cost. Final graphics can wait until the formula, quantity and claims are confirmed.

faqs.q: Can better packaging help on marketplaces?
faqs.a: Yes. A pack that reads clearly at small sizes improves the main listing image, and we prepare renders for your listings. Our notes for [e-commerce and D2C brands](/industries/ecommerce-d2c) cover the wider marketing picture.

faqs.q: Do you redesign existing packs or only create new ones?
faqs.a: Both. A redesign often keeps what customers already recognize, such as a color, shape or logo position, while fixing legibility, the compliance layout and variant confusion. [Tell us about your product](/contact) and we will suggest which route fits.
